clue.text: Stupid individuals. — persons put in a good man's charge

parts.note: asses are foolish, stupid people

indicators.note: the persons are placed inside the abbreviation for the good man

parts.note: ST, short for saint, is the crossword's good man
men are persons, people

explanation.surface: Foolish people are being handed over to the care of a virtuous guardian.
explanation.walkthrough: 'charge' is a noun here, a levy, not custody; the 's after 'good man' is a link, and 'put in' is the container signal.
explanation.definitionFit: An assessment is a sum levied, such as a tax or fee, so it is a charge in the financial sense.

clue.text: Make sure nothing inside is decrepit

indicators.note: inside places the word for nothing within the word for making sure

parts.note: to see that something happens is to make sure of it
nil means nothing, zero

explanation.surface: Check that nothing within is falling apart.
explanation.definitionFit: Senile describes the frailty and mental decline of old age, worn-out like something dilapidated.

clue.text: Without a synonym.

parts.note: reads as a word with no equivalent, but asks for a word meaning outside, which is the old sense of without

explanation.definitionFit: Without in its old sense means outside, so a word meaning outer is its synonym.

clue.text: Chose to give voice — escorted from the scene!

parts.note: to sing is to give voice
led out means guided away or escorted out

explanation.surface: A performer chose to sing and was then shown off the stage.
explanation.definitionFit: To single out is to pick one from a group, to select.

clue.text: Copy out once pamphlet appears

parts.note: ex means former or once, as in ex-wife
a tract is a short pamphlet, often religious

explanation.surface: Copying something out once a leaflet is published.
explanation.definitionFit: To extract a passage is to take it from a text and reproduce it elsewhere.

clue.text: Vehicle having separate back

indicators.note: back means the word for separate is read in reverse

parts.note: to part is to separate

explanation.surface: A vehicle is fitted with a detachable rear section.
explanation.walkthrough: A trap is a light two-wheeled horse-drawn carriage.
explanation.definitionFit: A trap is a small horse-drawn carriage, a means of transport.

clue.text: Sweet over unkind note

parts.note: past means over, finished
ill as in ill-natured, unkind
E is a musical note

explanation.surface: A sweet person gets over a nasty letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A pastille is a small lozenge or candy, a type of confectionery.

clue.text: Race date is concealed — but it gets out

indicators.note: concealed suggests the words are disguised, their letters rearranged so they are not seen as written

explanation.surface: The date of the race was kept secret, but the news leaked.
explanation.walkthrough: 'concealed' signals the letters of RACE DATE IS in disguise; 'but it' links to the definition, which reads as news leaking.
explanation.definitionFit: To eradicate is to root out or remove completely.

clue.text: Before parking carriage engineers make good any damage

indicators.note: Before tells us the parking letter goes ahead of the carriage word

parts.note: RE stands for the Royal Engineers, the British army corps
P is the map and road-sign abbreviation for parking
air in the sense of bearing or deportment, how one carries oneself

explanation.surface: Engineers, having parked a carriage, set about mending whatever was broken.
explanation.walkthrough: 'carriage' is not a vehicle but bearing, an AIR; the engineers' RE goes at the front.
explanation.definitionFit: To repair something is to fix it, restoring it after harm.

clue.text: Gut reaction shown this month in court

parts.note: INST, short for instant, means of the current month in old business letters

explanation.surface: A gut feeling turned up in a court case this month.
explanation.walkthrough: INST (instant) is old commercial shorthand for 'of this month', as in 'your letter of the 5th inst'.
explanation.definitionFit: Instinct is an intuitive, unreasoned response, the kind felt in the stomach.

clue.text: Left in the long grass, so it's said

indicators.note: in places the word for left inside the word for the tall grass

parts.note: a reed is a tall grass of wet places
port is the left side of a ship

explanation.surface: Something was abandoned in the tall grass, or so the story goes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Left' reads as abandoned but is the ship's left side; 'in' is the container signal and 'so it's' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Reported means stated or related by others, as in news passed on.

clue.text: A Quaker — sound writer

indicators.note: sound tells us the word for writer is heard rather than spelt

parts.note: a pen is a writing instrument

explanation.surface: A Quaker turns out to be a reliable author.
explanation.walkthrough: William Penn, the Quaker, founded Pennsylvania; his name is said just like PEN.
explanation.definitionFit: William Penn was a famous member of the Society of Friends, the religious group nicknamed Quakers.

clue.text: Official advertisement about pig-feed

indicators.note: about means the first word goes round the second

parts.note: a poster is a printed advertisement
mast is fallen beech nuts and acorns, used to feed pigs

explanation.surface: A bureaucrat puts up a notice concerning food for swine.
explanation.walkthrough: MAST is the nuts of forest trees on which pigs are fattened.
explanation.definitionFit: A postmaster is the official in charge of a post office.

clue.text: Nice chapel characters — brainy too

indicators.note: the letters, or characters, of the two words are taken and rearranged into new order

explanation.surface: The people attending a chapel in Nice are clever as well.
explanation.walkthrough: 'characters' looks like people but signals the letters of NICE CHAPEL, which are rearranged; 'too' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Encephalic means relating to the brain, which 'brainy' is stretched to mean in a playful way.

clue.text: March, though in favour of giving up

parts.note: pro means for, in favour of
cession is the act of ceding or giving up

explanation.surface: A protest march, even if it means supporting surrender.
explanation.walkthrough: 'March' is not the month but a parade; 'though' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: A procession is a body of people moving forward in orderly formation, as in a parade.

clue.text: Superficial Shakespearian. justice

definitions.meaning: Justice ... is the country magistrate in Henry IV Part 2 and The Merry Wives of Windsor

explanation.surface: A shallow-minded judge from one of Shakespeare's plays.
explanation.definitionFit: A superficial person lacks depth; Shakespeare named a foolish country justice for that quality.

clue.text: Protestant's article calling for reform left out

parts.note: an is the indefinite article

indicators.note: for reform means the remaining letters are re-formed into a new order
out tells us the letter for left is dropped from the word calling

explanation.surface: A Protestant's newspaper piece urging change was cut.
explanation.walkthrough: 'left out' drops one L from the fodder, leaving CALING; 'for reform' rearranges that. The 's is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Anglicans belong to the Church of England, a Protestant denomination.

clue.text: Most imaginative, putting the aged in A1 housing

indicators.note: housing means the first word holds the second inside it

parts.note: A1 means first-rate, the best
the aged are old

explanation.surface: The most creative idea is to put elderly people in first-class homes.
explanation.walkthrough: A1 means first-class; 'housing' is the container signal and 'putting' a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Boldest means most daring and adventurous, as in a bold, inventive plan.

clue.text: The sort of air Arne's lass sang?

definitions.text: The sort of air Arne's lass sang?

parts.words: The sort of air Arne's lass sang?
parts.note: plays on Thomas Arne's song The Lass with the ... Air, reading air as a tune rather than a manner

explanation.definitionFit: The adjective in the song's title describes a dainty, refined manner, which the clue reinterprets as a type of tune.

clue.text: Pull the girl up — she's so slow!

indicators.note: up in a down clue means the whole run is read from bottom to top

parts.note: to drag is to pull
gal is an informal word for a girl

explanation.surface: Someone hauls a dawdling girl along.
explanation.walkthrough: 'up' reverses DRAGGAL as a whole, giving the answer; 'she's so' is link and colour.
explanation.definitionFit: A laggard is one who falls behind, so as an adjective it means sluggish.

clue.text: Judge arranging a grim test — a reconstruction

indicators.note: arranging tells us the letters of the following words are put in a new order

explanation.surface: A judge sets up a tough test as a re-enactment of events.
explanation.walkthrough: 'arranging' shuffles A GRIM TEST plus A; 'reconstruction' backs up that rearrangement.
explanation.definitionFit: A magistrate is a lower-court official who presides over cases, a kind of justice.

clue.text: Girl trainee joins a sea-going vessel

parts.note: L stands for learner, as on British learner-driver plates
SS stands for steamship

explanation.surface: A young woman in training signs on to a ship.
explanation.definitionFit: Lass is a Scottish and northern English word for a young woman.

clue.text: Attack the man setting the rate

definitions.meaning: a sudden seizure or fit, as of apoplexy
the oarsman nearest the stern who sets the rowing pace for the crew

explanation.surface: Assaulting the person who decides the price.
explanation.definitionFit: A stroke is a sudden seizure; in rowing it is also the oarsman who sets the crew's pace.

clue.text: Warrant officer wearying-but smiling

parts.note: SM, sergeant major, is a warrant officer rank in the British army
irking means annoying or tiring someone

explanation.surface: A warrant officer is tiresome, yet wears a grin.
explanation.walkthrough: 'but' is a link between the wordplay and the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Smirking is smiling in a smug or self-satisfied way.

clue.text: Lacking employment, some become avid letter-writers

indicators.note: some means only part of the following words is used, a run of their letters

explanation.surface: Out of work, some people take up writing letters keenly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'become' is a link; the run sits across 'avid letter'.
explanation.definitionFit: Idle means not working, without a job or occupation.

clue.text: A trouble-maker's peculiar gait with backward roll

indicators.note: peculiar means odd, so the letters of gait are turned into a strange new order
backward means the word for roll is read from the end to the start

parts.note: a rota is a roll or list of names on duty

explanation.surface: A rabble-rouser has an odd walk with a rolling swagger.
explanation.walkthrough: 'peculiar' turns GAIT into AGIT; 'backward' turns ROTA into ATOR. The 's is 'is', a link.
explanation.definitionFit: An agitator stirs up public unrest, someone who causes disturbance.

clue.text: Gloss over

parts.note: reads as concealing a fault, but means literally coating something with a hard shiny glaze

explanation.definitionFit: To enamel a surface is to coat it with a glassy shiny finish, literally putting a gloss over it.

clue.text: Conclude cross is at risk

parts.note: to end is to conclude
cross means angry, so angered

explanation.surface: Finishing off a cross is a hazardous business.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cross' is an adjective meaning annoyed, not a crucifix; 'is' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Something endangered is in danger, threatened with harm.
